parole.significato: used to form the feminine of a masculine noun indicating nationality or ethnicity
parole.testo: From Slavic -ojka, compare Serbo-Croatian -ojka, or a combination of the feminine suffix -oaie (from Latin -ōnea; compare also Aromanian -oanji) and diminutive feminine suffix -că, from Old Church Slavonic -ъка (-ŭka), from Proto-Slavic *-ъka.

Possibly from Slavic *bezъmъ, compare Ukrainian безматок (bezmatok, “hive without a queen”). Another proposed etymology is from Vulgar Latin amphisbēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀμφισβητικός (amphisbētikós, “fond of disputing, contentious”) (compare Italian bisbetico). Compare also the variant dezmetic
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *bobrъ.

parole.significato: Carpathian toothwort (Cardamine glanduligera; synonyms: Dentaria glandulosa, Cardamine glandulosa)
parole.testo: Unknown. Either a substratum word, from Slavic, or less likely from Latin verbena.

parole.significato: a support structure made of two connected pieces of wood, used to transport a plough
parole.testo: Taken from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *kobyla (“mare”).
Uncertain. Possibly related to Slavic *kokorь, *kokora.
From a Slavic komora, itself ultimately a borrowing from Latin camera (“room”). Doublet of cameră and cămară.

parole.significato: to defeat, overcome, overwhelm, get the better of
parole.testo: Probably from a Slavic *povъršiti (“to overwhelm, weigh down”), with a change of prefix as with covârni < povârni, or due to influence from cotropi or other words beginning with 'co-'. Cf. also vârf.
Unknown. Probably of Slavic origin. Compare Serbo-Croatian kratica (“shortening”).
Uncertain. Possibly from a Slavic source (compare Polish kręty, Serbo-Croatian krut), from a Vulgar Latin root *cirricius, from cirrus, or a root *cricius, from Ancient Greek.

Possibly from a Common Slavic *kъmotrъ < Latin compater. However, the corresponding forms in other Slavic languages are different, such as Bulgarian, Croatian, Russian kum, Serbian kumak, which leads some linguists to propose that the Romanian word may have been derived analogically as a masculine f
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *kъrdo, from Proto-Indo-European *kerdʰ-. Doublet of cireadă and ciurdă. Compare Serbo-Croatian кр̏до/kȑdo (“herd”), English herd.
From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian dospjeti.
From hohot or from Slavic *xoxotati. However, as both words are expressive creations, they may also possibly be coincidental.
From a Slavic *živьcь, cf. Carpathian Rusyn живец (žyvec).
Probably of Slavic origin – compare the descendants of Proto-Slavic *lososь – but the derivation is not clear.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *màzati (“to smear, to anoint”).
From Slavic *mirosati or directly from Greek μυρώνω (myróno). Compare Megleno-Romanian miruses.

Uncertain. Probably of Slavic origin, compare Proto-Slavic *mogyla (“sepulchral cairn”), or an expressive creation based on the root moc-. The word found in Slavic languages seems itself to be of foreign origin. There have been attempts to link it to a Gepid word, but this is unlikely. Compare also

parole.significato: un-; de- (attached to past participles, gerundives and some adjectives to negate them)
parole.testo: Probably of Slavic origin, possibly borrowed from Old Church Slavonic не- (ne-) or some other language (cf. Bulgarian and Serbo-Croatian не-), from Proto-Slavic *ne. Less likely, originally from Latin ne-, and reinforced or influenced by the Slavic prefix. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né.
From Slavic. Compare Bulgarian намол (namol); possibly Polish namuł, Carpathian Rusyn намул (namul), Ukrainian намул (namul).
Origin disputed. Possibly from a Slavic language, akin to Albanian ulok.
Borrowed from Slavic. Compare Ukrainian плавні (plavni, “reed”).

parole.significato: hair left to grow past the shoulders or hang down the back
parole.testo: Appears to be a derivative of Romanian împleti (“to knit”). Compare Aromanian pleati. Some speculate derived from Slavic *pletъ (see *plesti (“to weave, plait”)).

parole.significato: ladle (deep-bowled spoon with a long, usually curved, handle)
parole.testo: From a Common Slavic *polonikъ, compare Ukrainian поло́ник (polónyk).
From a Slavic language, probably from *tovarъ (“loading”), contaminated with *podъvora (“stretcher”).
From a Slavic language; cf. Serbo-Croatian povrnuti (“to twist around”).
Unknown. Possibly from Common Slavic *prěmo (“from a region”) with a j added due to influence from jur or from Serbo-Croatian préžda ("in front, ahead").

parole.significato: an instrument used to perforate or make holes
parole.testo: From a Slavic *pribojь, cf. Slovene preboj.
Of Slavic origin; compare Carpathian Rusyn прыморозок (prŷmorozok, “hoarfrost”), Russian поморок (pomorok, “dense fog”).

Unknown. Influenced by râu (“river”), compare Megleno-Romanian păroi. Possibly from a Slavic language (compare Bulgarian порој). Alternative theories suggest Albanian përrua, Thracian *parau(t) and Greek *παρροή (*parroḯ), from παραρροή (pararroḯ).
Borrowed from Slavic. Compare Hungarian pózna.
Probably from Slavic *rapa (“swelling, bump, sore, wound”), or less likely *svrabъ (“scabies, itch”). Other proposed etymologies include medieval German Rapfe or Gepid *rappôns.
Probably of Slavic origin.
From a Common Slavic *jьskretąti (“to break”) or alternatively *sъkrenati (“to deviate”). Compare Serbo-Croatian skretati.
Unknown. Possibly an expressive creation or from a Slavic language.

Unknown. Probably from a Slavic language, compare *sъtęgъ. The alternate etymology of Vulgar Latin root *stangula, of Germanic origin, does not seem possible. http://dexonline.ro/search.php?cuv=stinghie.

Uncertain, but probably from a Slavic language; cf. Polish strój (“garment, clothing, attire”), Slovene srajca (“shirt”). When entering Romanian, it may have been taken as a diminutive (cf. the form străiță), and then later evolved to its current form. Compare Aromanian stranj, stranjiu (“clothing,

parole.significato: fathom or an old unit of measurement for length
parole.testo: From a Slavic *sęžьnь, probably contaminated with *sъtęženъ (cf. stânjeni).

parole.significato: to hinder, trouble, hamper, impede, interfere, disrupt, disturb, interrupt
parole.testo: From a Slavic *sъtęžiti or from *sъtęgnǫti, participle of *sъtęženъ. Cf. also stânjen.
Most likely from a Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian сур (sur), Serbo-Croatian sur. A less likely etymology connects it to Latin syrus, or links it with Italian soro.
Borrowed from Slavic *taborъ, from Hungarian tábor, from a Turkic language.

parole.significato: throwing of a net for fishing
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian ton, also Ukrainian, Russian тоня (tonja).
Probably from a Common Slavic *trǫtъ (“drone”).
Of Slavic origin; from Serbo-Croatian vlaga (“moisture”); compare Aromanian vlagã (“moisture”). Perhaps was confused with Slavic *voldъ (“power”) in Romanian.

parole.significato: to bewilder, astound, confuse, befuddle, fluster
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Common Slavic *zapačiti (“to make something spin”), or an expressive creation based on zap.

parole.significato: to take shape; to come into being; start
parole.testo: Possibly from the variant form, înciripa, from a Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian čerep (“pot”), though the semantic link is unclear. Another possibility is a link to fire.
From the variant form năbuși < Common Slavic *nabušiti.

From a Slavic language (compare Serbo-Croatian škȏla, Bulgarian школа (škola), Polish szkoła, Russian шко́ла (škóla)), themselves taken from Latin schola, ultimately from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
Of Slavic origin; compare Serbo-Croatian ševar, Ukrainian шувар (šuvar). Cf. also Aromanian shuvar.

Borrowed from a South Slavic (a)ciganinŭ (cf. Church Slavonic циганинъ (ciganinŭ)), from early modern Greek τσιγγάνος (tsingános) or ατσίγγανος (atsínganos), variant of Byzantine Greek ἀθίγγανος (athínganos, “untouchable”)(a compound of privative ἀ- (a-) + θιγγάνω (thingánō, “to touch”)), used also

Uncertain. Possibly from Latin boreās (“northern wind”) (compare Italian borea, Dalmatian and Venetan bura, also Catalan boira and Albanian borë) or alternatively Slavic (Proto-Slavic *buřa; compare Serbo-Croatian bura, Bulgarian буря (burja), Macedonian бура (bura)).

parole.significato: layer; peel (of fruit), rind, crust (of bread), shell (of nuts), or bark (of trees)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кожа (koža), or from a (South) Slavic koža, from Proto-Slavic *koža. Compare Serbo-Croatian ко̏жа, Bulgarian кожа (koža). Compare also Aromanian coaji.
Unknown. Probably an expressive creation, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *contorpīre, from Latin contorpere, from torpere, or alternatively a Common Slavic *otrabiti (“to cut”).

Uncertain. Probably a substratum word. Other theories include a Vulgar Latin root *curtiāre (“cut”), from Latin curtāre, or a *cruciāre (“cross”), from crux or a *curatiāre; alternatively, there may be a connection with Slavic *krotiti (compare ocroti). Compare also the likely related Albanian kurse

parole.significato: young horse (up to three years old)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *caballānus, diminutive of Latin caballus, or from carnalis. Compare also Spanish carnero. Scriban (1939) proposes Transylvanian Saxon Jêrlänk, which is cognate to German Jährling and English yearling. Other theories include a Slavic *kъrdlanъ or a pre-Roma

parole.significato: a class of Romanian folk songs, often melancholic and expressing sorrow, pain, longing, wistfulness or other such stron…
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly of Slavic origin, such as Serbo-Croatian daljina ("distance; removing, furthering, distancing"); compare the phonetic transition from Serbo-Croatian haljina to haină, and see also the semantic development of Portuguese saudade. Less likely etymologies proposed include Middle High G

Unknown. Probably from a Common Slavic *gadati through an intermediate *gadačь (“guesser”), or from a Germanic language (Gothic or Gepidic), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gitisōną, whence English guess.

Uncertain; possibly a substratum word, akin to Albanian grihë, or derived from Albanian gërresë (“potter's instrument for leveling”). Alternatively, from a Slavic *kresь or *gresь; compare Serbo-Croatian kresalo, kresivo (“flint, tinderbox”), kresati (“light with flint”), kresiti (“set off sparks”).

parole.significato: to chop off, cut off, hew off, lop off, sever, dock, cut
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from Common Slavic *rězati (“shorten”), but this presents phonetic difficulties. Another possibility may be a Vulgar Latin root *retizāre (“cut branches hanging above water”) < Latin retae, or *retundiāre (compare French rogner), or from Ancient Greek αἱρετίζω (hairetízō) ("to choos

parole.significato: nappy, diaper (an absorbent garment worn by a baby, or by someone who is incontinent.)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Slavic *skutъ, or from Vulgar Latin *scuticum, from Latin scutica (“a leather lash, whip”) (itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σκύτος (skútos)), and probably confused with derivatives of cutis (“leather”) (compare cutica). Origin uncertain. Many theories have been proposed. Possibly a singularised plural of strug (now a regional term found in Bessarabia), which may be related to strung (“lathe”), strunji or the verb struji (“to clean feathers, branches, cobs of corn, etc.; to shave or scrape off; to chisel”), a region
Possibly borrowed from Common Slavic. Compare Bulgarian търг (tărg). Alternatively from a Balkan substrate.

Origin unknown. Possibly of expressive origin. Other theories provide difficulties: from Slavic burda; from Vulgar Latin *exvŏlĭtāre, alternatively from *abhorrĭdus; based on bord; or, from German Bürde.
